query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Simultaneous mechanical wear and elevated-temperature corrosion accelerates degradation in the multi‐phase eutectic high‐entropy alloy because the wear process continuously removes the protective passive oxide film at the heterogeneous phase boundaries, which then exposes fresh, electrochemically dissimilar surfaces that promote micro‐galvanic corrosion.
generation.material_initial_state: A multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy with well-developed phase boundaries and initially stable passive oxide films covering each phase.
generation.intervention: Expose the alloy to simultaneous mechanical wear (e.g., sliding wear) and a corrosive environment at elevated temperature versus exposing similar samples to isolated wear or isolated corrosion.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperature where oxide formation and removal dynamics are active; the presence of a standardized corrosive medium (e.g., chloride-containing solution or gas) and controlled wear conditions (consistent sliding load and speed) with maintained humidity and pH.
generation.structural_mediator: Interfaces between the dissimilar phases; these boundaries lose their protective oxide layer from mechanical wear, becoming sites for intensified micro-galvanic activity.
generation.mechanism: Mechanical removal of the passive oxide film at phase boundaries exposes chemically active surfaces. The potential difference between the dissimilar phases establishes micro-galvanic cells, which accelerate localized corrosion. This corrosion weakens the material structure and, in turn, further enhances the susceptibility to additional wear, forming a synergistic cycle of degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to baseline conditions (isolated wear or corrosion), the alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion is expected to show a noticeably higher overall degradation rate. In particular, the corrosion rate is predicted to be significantly elevated beyond simple additive effects, while wear depth may increase modestly due to the compromised integrity of the now-corroded interface.
generation.baseline: Alloy samples subjected to either wear-only (in an inert environment) or corrosion-only (without mechanical disruption) tests at the same elevated temperature.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable for eutectic high-entropy alloys with heterogeneous phase electrochemical potentials under elevated temperature conditions that allow for repeated oxide film formation and removal. It may not apply to alloys with uniform corrosion behavior or under low-temperature conditions where passive films remain stable.
generation.uncertainty: The specific magnitude of the synergistic enhancement in degradation and the precise wear-to-corrosion contribution ratio remain uncertain until further empirical data is collected.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical eutectic high-entropy alloy samples and divide them into three test groups: (1) simultaneous exposure to wear and corrosion at high temperature, (2) wear-only exposure at high temperature in an inert atmosphere, and (3) corrosion-only exposure at high temperature with no mechanical wear. Monitor each group's degradation over a fixed period using standardized measurements.
measurements: Wear track depth and morphology (via profilometry and SEM)
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) to assess corrosion rates and passive film integrity
Surface composition and evidence of galvanic coupling (via EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the simultaneous wear-corrosion group does not exhibit a degradation rate significantly higher than the sum of the individual wear-only and corrosion-only groups, particularly lacking evidence of disrupted passive films and enhanced micro-galvanic corrosion at phase boundaries, then the hypothesis—that wear-induced removal of passive film at heterogeneous interfaces drives the synergistic degradation—is falsified.
